title: No choice but to shoot: judge - Winnipeg Free Press
subtitle: Breaking News, Sports, Manitoba, Canada
article: Hey there, time traveller!
This article was published 21/07/2009 (5884 days ago), so information in it may no longer be current.
He was caught in the act of stabbing his roommate to death - and then fatally shot by police when he refused to drop the blood-soaked knife.
Now a Manitoba judge has weighed in on the tragic case, saying police had no choice but to use lethal force when confronted with a horrific scene inside a Portage Avenue apartment suite.

Zunga Bashir, 21, died of a single gunshot wound to his abdomen. Four officers had been called to a Portage Avenue apartment block on the night of Dec. 30, 2005 and arrived to find Bashir repeatedly stabbing James David as he lay on a couch. David suffered approximately 40 separate wounds to his throat and chest and was pronounced dead at hospital.

"Although we would all wish that someone would risk their life to save that of our family member, police officers have families, too. They are not paid or trained to risk their lives. They are trained to preserve lives," provincial court Judge Judith Elliott wrote in a 30-page report released Monday.
"Zunga Bashir was in the process of stabbing another person to death. Officers involved had a duty to stop that. They ordered (him) to stop and if he had complied, he would be alive today."
Elliott took the rare step of making no recommendations in her report.

Bashir and David were good friends who were living together at the time. They were drinking on the night of the incident and got into an argument because Bashir thought David was making "unwanted advances" to his female friend, court was told.
Several people called police to report a fight in progress. Officers arrived quickly and had to break the door down when nobody answered.
The room was dark and police initially thought Bashir was stabbing at an empty piece of furniture. They realized it was a person as they got closer.
"Drop the knife. Don't be stupid, drop the knife," one officer yelled at him. Police say Bashir continued to make stabbing motions towards the victim

"I yelled at the male to drop the knife. Mr. Bashir did not respond,," said the officer who shot Bashir. "He started to raise the knife and as he did he started yelling and the knife came forward. He appeared to be either attacking myself or the victim or my partner."

The officer fired a single shot to Bashir's "centre of mass" - exactly as police are trained. Two use-of-force experts testified at the inquest that the officer "did not have any other option" and acted properly. Although police were not equipped with Tasers at the time, the experts said using one "would not have been realistic" under the circumstances.

Members of the Bashir family were granted standing at the inquest and submitted a written statement. They disagreed with the actions of police and the judge's findings. "We feel the whole story and the circumstances in which the police shot him will remain a mystery, except to those police officers who were involved," they wrote. "We recognize the late Zunga did wrong by stabbing another, but the police should not have been the prosecutor and the judge. The police prosecuted him, pass death sentence on him and shot him dead."

The family said police should have tried to disarm Bashir without shooting him. Elliott disagreed, saying that likely would have resulted in serious injuries or even death to one or more of the officers.

Sensitivity was lacking, inquest finds
WINNIPEG police showed a disturbing lack of sensitivity when dealing with the brother of a man they'd shot and killed, an inquest has concluded.
Provincial court Judge Judith Elliott expressed concerns about police conduct in her written report released Monday. She said the issue was not "central to the inquest" but needed to be addressed.

Larry Bashir was detained by police for questioning around 2 a.m. His brother, Zunga, died about an hour later. Police didn't tell him or any other family members until after 7:30 a.m., when they still had him sitting in an empty interview room at the Public Safety Building.
Elliott said there was no reason for the delay, especially since the brother wasn't considered a key witness.

"During the time he was in police custody, Mr. Bashir's brother was dying - yet he was neither facilitated in going to the hospital nor told what was happening so that he could contact other family members to do so," said Elliott. "I realize there was a complicated investigation going on, concerning both a homicide and a police shooting, and that there were many officers involved. However, I believe a more compassionate approach was called for."

Larry Bashir also testified that officers appeared to be "laughing and joking" and treating the incident "very casually." Family members complained about the treatment in a letter they wrote to the court.
- MIke McIntyre
